segments.source: Formal methods do not remove the specification problem. If we prove that an image classifier does not change its label for any perturbation within a small norm ball, we have proved a precise property. We have not proved that the classifier understands the object, that the perturbation model reflects realistic changes, or that the system will behave safely when its camera fails. Formal verification closes one logical gap while leaving the modeling gap intact.

Testing is broad but incomplete. Verification is complete but narrow. A mature assurance strategy combines them. Formal analysis can protect invariants that are crisp enough to specify, such as access-control constraints, output ranges, safety envelopes, or deterministic policy rules. Stress testing can explore semantic and sociotechnical behaviors that are difficult to formalize, such as manipulation, bias, hallucination, or user overreliance. Monitoring then catches failures that neither pre-deployment method anticipated.

Many important AI failures occur in code that is far easier to verify than the neural network. Data validation, unit conversion, thresholding, access-control checks, routing logic, aggregation, schema transformations, and post-processing can be specified precisely. A trustworthy architecture should exploit this asymmetry. The less critical logic is hidden inside a language model prompt, the more of the system can be subjected to conventional testing, type checking, static analysis, and formal verification.

This also changes how evidence is designed. Build a testing pyramid with fast deterministic checks at the base, statistical behavior tests above them, adversarial and end-to-end scenarios at the system layer, and monitored field performance at the top. Every release should know which claim each test supports. Evidence should be collected at the level at which a claim can be falsified. Averages are helpful for orientation, but engineers need slices, counterexamples, traces, thresholds and failure cases when those are what determine whether authority should be granted. The most valuable evaluation is often not the one with the most samples; it is the one that can cause the team to change a release decision because it directly exercises an assumption on which the system depends.

A useful discipline is to separate capability evidence from assurance evidence. Capability evidence asks whether the system can perform a task under some conditions. Assurance evidence asks whether it can be relied upon for a specified purpose, which also requires information about failure behavior, detection, containment, human response and change over time. The distinction becomes increasingly important for general-purpose models because impressive competence on difficult benchmarks can coexist with surprisingly simple failures. A trustworthy system needs an account of both sides of that jagged performance profile.
segments.translation: O disciplină utilă este separarea dovezilor de capabilitate de dovezile de asigurare. Dovezile de capabilitate întreabă dacă sistemul poate îndeplini o sarcină în anumite condiții. Dovezile de asigurare întreabă dacă ne putem baza pe el pentru un scop specificat, ceea ce necesită și informații despre comportamentul în caz de eșec, detectare, limitarea efectelor, reacția umană și schimbarea în timp. Distincția devine tot mai importantă pentru modelele cu scop general, deoarece competența impresionantă în teste de referință dificile poate coexista cu eșecuri surprinzător de simple. Un sistem demn de încredere are nevoie de o descriere a ambelor laturi ale acestui profil de performanță inegal.

segments.source: The boundary of the claim must remain visible. No test suite covers an open input space. Passing tests can create false confidence when test construction, data provenance or scenario diversity is weak. This is not pedantry. Learned systems are deployed in open environments, and evidence can expire when data, users, models, prompts, tools or incentives change. Good engineering documentation therefore says not only what passed, but what was not tested, what assumptions make the result meaningful, what observations would contradict it and what change would force the evidence to be collected again.

There is also an organisational dimension. A control that exists in a design document but is routinely bypassed is not an effective control; a human approval that receives no useful evidence is not independent oversight; a red-team finding that cannot block a release is not a meaningful safety signal. Trustworthiness becomes real only when measurements are connected to authority. This is why the course repeatedly returns to owners, escalation, rollback, incident review and evidence freshness alongside model metrics.
segments.translation: Există și o dimensiune organizațională. O măsură de control care există într-un document de proiectare, dar este ocolită în mod curent, nu este eficientă; o aprobare umană care nu primește dovezi utile nu reprezintă supraveghere independentă; o constatare red-team care nu poate bloca o lansare nu reprezintă un semnal de siguranță semnificativ. Caracterul demn de încredere devine real numai când măsurările sunt conectate la autoritate. De aceea, cursul revine constant la responsabili, escaladare, revenirea la o versiune anterioară, analiza incidentelor și actualitatea dovezilor, alături de metricile modelului.

segments.source: For Meridian, its regression pipeline distinguishes code-level policy tests, retrieval quality tests, factuality evaluations, injection red teams and shadow-deployment telemetry. A failed high-severity control test blocks release even when aggregate model quality improves. The running system is deliberately ordinary rather than futuristic. Its importance lies in how small product decisions accumulate: adding a repository changes privacy assumptions; adding a tool changes the threat model; adding memory changes persistence; adding autonomy changes the cost of an error. The same pattern occurs in production AI systems across domains. Architecture and governance determine whether a model weakness remains a recoverable inconvenience or becomes a consequential failure.

The engineering takeaway is therefore deliberately conservative. Do not ask a method to establish more than it can. Combine heterogeneous evidence when failure mechanisms differ, preserve counter-evidence instead of averaging it away, and make safe fallback part of the normal design rather than an emergency afterthought. Trust is a human attitude; trustworthy engineering is the work of making reliance inspectable, bounded and revisable.

Combinați dovezi eterogene când mecanismele de eșec diferă, păstrați dovezile contrare în loc să le estompați prin mediere și includeți alternativa sigură de rezervă în proiectarea normală, nu ca pe o soluție de urgență adăugată ulterior. Încrederea este o atitudine umană; ingineria demnă de încredere presupune munca de a face utilizarea unui sistem inspectabilă, limitată și revizuibilă.

segments.source: A second way to reason about a testing pyramid for AI systems is through counterfactual deployment review. Imagine that the system fails tomorrow in a way that is costly but entirely plausible. Which log would explain the event? Which test should have anticipated it? Which component could have contained it? Which person had authority to reduce exposure before the incident? Working backwards from those questions exposes assurance gaps that are invisible in a model-centric review. It also turns abstract principles into engineering requirements: observability, provenance, reversibility and clear ownership are not administrative extras; they are mechanisms for learning from uncertainty without allowing every failure to become a crisis.

The strongest teams also distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence. If a red team did not discover a failure, that is evidence about the search that was performed, not a proof that the failure is impossible. If a subgroup has too few examples to estimate performance, reporting the aggregate score does not resolve the uncertainty. If a formal verifier proves one invariant, it does not certify properties outside the formal model. This epistemic discipline may look modest, but it is one of the most important differences between trustworthy engineering and assurance theater.
segments.translation: Cele mai solide echipe disting și absența dovezilor de dovada absenței. Dacă o echipă red-team nu a descoperit un eșec, aceasta oferă dovezi despre căutarea efectuată, nu o dovadă că eșecul este imposibil. Dacă un subgrup are prea puține exemple pentru estimarea performanței, raportarea scorului agregat nu rezolvă incertitudinea. Dacă un verificator formal demonstrează un invariant, el nu certifică proprietăți aflate în afara modelului formal. Această disciplină epistemică poate părea modestă, dar este una dintre cele mai importante diferențe dintre ingineria demnă de încredere și simulacrul de asigurare.

segments.source: For a design review, a testing pyramid for AI systems can be turned into a short evidence exercise. Start with one concrete claim the team expects to make at release, then list three plausible observations that would make the claim false or materially weaker. Next, ask which of those observations can be generated before deployment, which require production monitoring, and which depend on information the organisation does not currently collect. The exercise is intentionally asymmetric: it is easier to accumulate confirmatory examples than to search for conditions that would change a decision. Designing the search for disconfirmation makes testing more realistic and creates explicit triggers for escalation or rollback.

For students and practitioners, this suggests a useful habit: write the decision rule beside the metric. If a score deteriorates by five percent, what happens? If a novel input is detected, who sees it? If two evaluators disagree, is the output blocked, sampled for review, or accepted? If the answer is 'nothing', the measurement is primarily descriptive. Trustworthy engineering begins when evidence participates in control flow and when the organisation can explain why a particular amount of residual uncertainty was acceptable for the authority that was granted.

Dacă răspunsul este „nimic”, măsurarea este în principal descriptivă. 8.2 Formal Methods, Verified Harnesses, and Runtime Assurance

A course on formal verification around AI should begin with the failure it is meant to prevent, not with the metric that happens to be fashionable. Formal methods are strongest where specifications and state spaces can be made precise. Complete verification of a large generative model is generally infeasible, but important surrounding properties can be verified or enforced: access-control logic, state machines, numeric robustness regions, protocol conformance and runtime safety invariants. This distinction matters because the same numerical result can support very different conclusions depending on the deployment context. The relevant question is always conditional: what exactly has been observed, under which assumptions, and which future decision is that evidence supposed to justify? Keeping those three parts together prevents a familiar failure of AI projects, in which a technically correct measurement is gradually retold as a much stronger claim than the experiment ever established.

Consider a tool-using agent whose natural-language plan is probabilistic while the action policy is a finite state machine that forbids payment without an approved invoice and human signature. The system does not require a proof of the model’s thoughts to prove the authorization rule. What makes the example useful is the separation between mechanism and symptom. The visible symptom may be an incorrect answer, an unfair alert, an unsafe action or a privacy leak, but the mechanism can sit in the data pipeline, model, retrieval layer, policy engine, user interface or organisational process. A trustworthy-AI investigation therefore resists the urge to repair the first component that looks suspicious. It reconstructs the path that produced the outcome and asks which intervention would actually break that path.

Large language models challenge current verification methods in several ways. Their state spaces are enormous, generation is stochastic, behavior depends on natural-language context, systems call external tools, and many desired properties are semantic. 'Never manipulate the user' or 'always give an adequate scientific explanation' is not yet a tractable formal property. Researchers are extending verification to broader neural operators and exploring verified explanations, but end-to-end semantic proof for frontier LLM systems is not close to routine engineering.

A practical direction is to put formally checkable structure around a probabilistic model. The model proposes; deterministic or symbolic components constrain what may happen. Examples include typed tool schemas, permission policies, finite-state workflows, rule engines, transaction limits, proof obligations, schema validators, resource budgets, and runtime monitors. The model remains uncertain, but critical transitions become explicitly governed. This architecture is especially important for agents, where the cost of an erroneous action can exceed the cost of an erroneous sentence.

One reason formal assurance is difficult is that engineers often do not know the right specification in advance. A pragmatic approach is iterative. Start with explicit invariants derived from policy and hazards. Use tests, red teams, and formal tools to find counterexamples. Refine the specification when a counterexample reveals an unmodeled condition. This resembles counterexample-guided abstraction refinement in formal methods, but the loop can also include human interpretation of semantic failures. The key idea is that specifications are learned and improved through falsification rather than treated as perfect at the start.

This also changes how evidence is designed. Push critical invariants into small, inspectable components, use model checking or theorem proving where specifications justify the effort, and combine them with runtime monitors that reject actions violating invariants. Treat the model as an untrusted proposer for security-critical transitions when possible. Evidence should be collected at the level at which a claim can be falsified. Averages are helpful for orientation, but engineers need slices, counterexamples, traces, thresholds and failure cases when those are what determine whether authority should be granted. The most valuable evaluation is often not the one with the most samples; it is the one that can cause the team to change a release decision because it directly exercises an assumption on which the system depends.

The distinction becomes increasingly important for general-purpose models because impressive competence on difficult benchmarks can coexist with surprisingly simple failures. A trustworthy system needs an account of both sides of that jagged performance profile.

segments.source: 8.3 Benchmarks, Contamination, LLM Judges, and External Validity

A course on evaluation validity should begin with the failure it is meant to prevent, not with the metric that happens to be fashionable. An evaluation has construct validity only when the measured task represents the capability or risk claimed. Data contamination, prompt sensitivity, benchmark saturation and narrow task definitions can separate score improvement from deployment improvement. LLM-as-judge methods add scale but also evaluator biases and correlated failure. This distinction matters because the same numerical result can support very different conclusions depending on the deployment context. The relevant question is always conditional: what exactly has been observed, under which assumptions, and which future decision is that evidence supposed to justify? Keeping those three parts together prevents a familiar failure of AI projects, in which a technically correct measurement is gradually retold as a much stronger claim than the experiment ever established.

Consider a model grading another model’s factuality while sharing similar training data and stylistic preferences. Agreement can look high because both systems reward fluent, agreeable answers, not because the evaluator independently establishes truth. What makes the example useful is the separation between mechanism and symptom. The visible symptom may be an incorrect answer, an unfair alert, an unsafe action or a privacy leak, but the mechanism can sit in the data pipeline, model, retrieval layer, policy engine, user interface or organisational process. A trustworthy-AI investigation therefore resists the urge to repair the first component that looks suspicious. It reconstructs the path that produced the outcome and asks which intervention would actually break that path.

The 2026 International AI Safety Report uses the term evaluation gap for the recurring mismatch between pre-deployment scores and real-world usefulness or risk. The gap exists because controlled tasks simplify the environment, because benchmark data can become familiar to developers, because users behave unpredictably, because real systems contain tools and retrieval components absent from model tests, and because long-horizon failures compound. The same pattern is visible in medical external validation and in current agent benchmarks.

A 2026 review of agentic-AI evaluation found that many benchmarks emphasize task completion while under-measuring safety, maintainability, workflow integration, process quality, and deployment cost. AgencyBench and related efforts push toward longer contexts and realistic multi-step tasks, but the core problem remains: a benchmark can sample only part of the operational distribution.

Evaluation should be designed to falsify the claim rather than confirm the system. If the claim is that an LLM provides grounded scientific answers, the test should contain adversarially ambiguous questions, missing evidence, conflicting sources, unfamiliar domains, and prompts that encourage unsupported certainty. If the claim is that an agent respects authorization boundaries, the test should include indirect prompt injection, ambiguous authority, stale credentials, malicious tool output, and tasks where the easiest path violates policy.

This also changes how evidence is designed. Protect hidden test data, refresh scenarios, use multiple evaluators, measure judge consistency and bias, require source-based or executable checks when available, include human adjudication for uncertain classes, and validate benchmark results against field outcomes. NIST TEVV-Athlon’s real-world orientation is useful as a design prompt rather than a replacement for domain expertise. Evidence should be collected at the level at which a claim can be falsified. A trustworthy system needs an account of both sides of that jagged performance profile.

9. Trustworthy Generative AI
Engineering question: How do we engineer systems whose natural output is plausible language rather than guaranteed truth?

Generative AI changes the shape of quality assurance. A classifier emits a bounded label; a language model can generate an unbounded claim, citation, plan, program or argument. The space of possible errors is correspondingly large, and fluent presentation can conceal weak evidence. The right response is not to demand impossible certainty from the model but to build pipelines that externalise evidence, verification and abstention. Meridian’s original use case now returns to the centre of the story: a research assistant must distinguish synthesis from invention.
9.1 Hallucination, Factuality, RAG, and Claim-Level Grounding

Engineers often encounter factuality in generative AI first as a vocabulary term and only later as a design problem. Hallucination is an umbrella term. Errors may arise because the model lacks knowledge, retrieval returns poor evidence, context is ignored, sources conflict, the model overgeneralises, or a citation is fabricated. Each mechanism suggests different diagnostics and mitigations. This distinction matters because the same numerical result can support very different conclusions depending on the deployment context. The relevant question is always conditional: what exactly has been observed, under which assumptions, and which future decision is that evidence supposed to justify? Keeping those three parts together prevents a familiar failure of AI projects, in which a technically correct measurement is gradually retold as a much stronger claim than the experiment ever established.

Consider a RAG system that retrieves the correct policy paragraph yet generates a conclusion not entailed by it. Retrieval recall is good, but grounding fails at generation. Conversely, a perfect generator cannot cite evidence that retrieval never supplied. What makes the example useful is the separation between mechanism and symptom. The visible symptom may be an incorrect answer, an unfair alert, an unsafe action or a privacy leak, but the mechanism can sit in the data pipeline, model, retrieval layer, policy engine, user interface or organisational process. A trustworthy-AI investigation therefore resists the urge to repair the first component that looks suspicious. It reconstructs the path that produced the outcome and asks which intervention would actually break that path.

The word hallucination covers several mechanisms: parametric memory can be wrong or incomplete; generation can combine true fragments into a false claim; retrieval can return irrelevant or stale evidence; the model can cite a source that does not support the sentence; ambiguity can be resolved incorrectly; and the model can answer when it should abstain. Mitigation depends on which mechanism is present.

Factuality benchmarks have improved by narrowing the task and improving ground truth. SimpleQA was designed around short questions with easily graded answers, while SimpleQA Verified in 2025 re-audited and rebalanced a subset to reduce label noise and redundancy. The broader lesson is that benchmark quality can matter as much as model quality. When the measurement target is factuality, weak reference data produces misleading progress.

RAG can improve factuality by giving a model access to external evidence, but it also creates new failure points. Retrieval may miss the relevant document. A malicious document may inject instructions. The model may cite a retrieved passage that does not entail its claim. The corpus may be stale. Permission filters may leak information across users. Trustworthy RAG therefore needs source provenance, retrieval evaluation, authorization, citation validation, update control, and a policy for what happens when evidence is absent or contradictory.

This also changes how evidence is designed. Separate retrieval evaluation from generation evaluation, segment outputs into checkable claims, attach evidence spans, test entailment or source support, and make unsupported claims visible. For high-value factual workflows, route unresolved claims to verification or abstention rather than asking the model to sound more cautious. Evidence should be collected at the level at which a claim can be falsified. Averages are helpful for orientation, but engineers need slices, counterexamples, traces, thresholds and failure cases when those are what determine whether authority should be granted. The most valuable evaluation is often not the one with the most samples; it is the one that can cause the team to change a release decision because it directly exercises an assumption on which the system depends.

A useful discipline is to separate capability evidence from assurance evidence. Capability evidence asks whether the system can perform a task under some conditions. Assurance evidence asks whether it can be relied upon for a specified purpose, which also requires information about failure behavior, detection, containment, human response and change over time. The distinction becomes increasingly important for general-purpose models because impressive competence on difficult benchmarks can coexist with surprisingly simple failures. A trustworthy system needs an account of both sides of that jagged performance profile.
segments.translation: O disciplină utilă este separarea dovezilor de capabilitate de dovezile de asigurare. Dovezile de capabilitate întreabă dacă sistemul poate îndeplini o sarcină în anumite condiții. Dovezile de asigurare întreabă dacă ne putem baza pe el pentru un scop specificat, ceea ce necesită și informații despre comportamentul în caz de eșec, detectare, limitarea efectelor, reacția umană și schimbarea în timp. Distincția devine tot mai importantă pentru modelele cu scop general, deoarece competența impresionantă în teste de referință dificile poate coexista cu eșecuri surprinzător de simple. Un sistem demn de încredere are nevoie de o descriere a ambelor laturi ale acestui profil de performanță inegal.

segments.source: The boundary of the claim must remain visible. RAG does not guarantee truth, and automated verifiers can share the generator’s weaknesses. Sources may themselves be outdated, malicious or contradictory. This is not pedantry. Learned systems are deployed in open environments, and evidence can expire when data, users, models, prompts, tools or incentives change. Good engineering documentation therefore says not only what passed, but what was not tested, what assumptions make the result meaningful, what observations would contradict it and what change would force the evidence to be collected again.

A citation at the end of a paragraph does not prove that every sentence is supported. Trustworthy factual generation benefits from claim segmentation: identify factual claims, retrieve candidate evidence, test whether the evidence entails or contradicts the claim, and preserve the source span. This can be implemented with a combination of retrieval, natural-language inference models, rule-based checks, and human review for difficult cases. The aim is to make unsupported claims detectable rather than to make generation itself magically truthful.
